editions.title: Fridge hacks spread across Europe as AMD posts record quarter
editions.notification: Supermarket fridges hacked across Europe, while AMD reports its best quarter ever.
editions.intro:
A suspected cyber-attack is spreading across Europe. Supermarket chains in at least seven countries, including Ahold Delhaize, Ikea, Carrefour Belgium and Colruyt, reported freezer temperatures rising overnight to as high as 50C, and some stores pulled chilled and frozen goods from sale. The EU food commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain, and experts warned that many refrigeration controllers are reachable online and unpatched. It follows a French attack last month that affected hundreds of supermarkets. The UK's AI minister said a serious cyber breach is "extremely likely", and the NCSC warned that British firms were wilfully blind to threats.

In markets, the story was chipmakers. AMD reported a record $13.4 billion quarter, with data centre revenue of $8.5 billion, and guided to about $17 billion next quarter, while Intel guided to $15-16 billion. Its shares rose about 5% after hours, and analysts see AMD possibly overtaking Intel as the largest x86 chip vendor. AMD's gaming revenue fell 40%, however, as memory shortages driven by AI demand squeeze consumer hardware. Apple also reported a record iPhone quarter of $57.58 billion, up 17%, despite no standard iPhone launch, though it warned of higher memory costs.

Political and market backdrop was volatile. Democrats swept key US midterm races, including Texas, and European and Asian tech shares fell on expectations of tougher scrutiny of Trump-era policies. US tech stocks recovered on Tuesday after the Nasdaq had entered correction territory on Monday. Oracle reportedly dropped a $7 billion Tencent AI deal under US pressure, a single-source report that is worth watching.

top_stories.title: Suspected cyber-attack hits fridges and freezers across Europe
top_stories.summary: Supermarkets in at least seven European countries reported freezer temperatures rising to as high as 50C overnight, with several firms confirming hacks. The EU food commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.

top_stories.title: AMD posts its largest and most profitable quarter
top_stories.summary: AMD reported record revenue of $13.4bn, with data centre making up about 63%, and forecast $17bn next quarter. Gaming revenue fell 40% as component shortages hit consumer sales, and AMD expects a down year for consumer markets in 2027.

top_stories.title: Apple posts iPhone sales record without a standard iPhone
top_stories.summary: iPhone revenue rose 17% to $57.58bn, driven by the pricier iPhone 18 Pro models and higher prices on older models. Total revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn, but Apple flagged higher memory costs.

top_stories.title: Democratic win rattles Trump-linked trades
top_stories.summary: A Democratic sweep of Congress unsettled global markets, with Asian tech shares falling, the dollar weakening and Treasuries rallying. Investors are pricing in tougher scrutiny of Trump's agenda across AI and crypto.

top_stories.title: PC makers shift production back to China
top_stories.summary: HP and Asus are moving some PC manufacturing from Thailand and Vietnam back to China, with Dell reportedly considering it too. Rising memory and processor costs, and IDC's 20.1% fall in Q3 PC shipments, are driving the shift.

top_stories.title: Drax plans AI datacentre at UK's biggest power plant
top_stories.summary: Drax has agreed a deal with Brookfield and Radiant for a datacentre at its North Yorkshire site, with potential investment above £20bn and eventual capacity over 1GW. Drax's market value rose almost 9%.

top_stories.title: Google makes AI opt-in for school students
top_stories.summary: Gemini and other AI features will be off by default for K-12 student accounts, and schools that keep AI disabled will lose access to Google Search. The move reverses an August decision and drew criticism from New York's mayor.

editions.title: Apple beats on iPhone as Anthropic's compute bill tops $1trn
editions.notification: Apple's iPhone sales hit a record without a standard iPhone. Anthropic's compute commitments near $1trn. Read the briefing.
editions.intro:
Apple dominated the day's financial news. Its fourth-quarter results showed iPhone revenue of $57.58bn, up 17% year on year, driven by the pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max and by price rises on older models. Total revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn, services reached $31.57bn and the Mac grew 24%, while iPad fell 10%. Chief executive John Ternus said memory costs were rising but partly offset. The foldable iPhone Duo, priced at $1,999, sold out quickly, and Apple said supply will be hard to predict. Apple's results are reported in the quarter to September, and its first full report under Ternus is due on 2 November.

The AI sector drew attention too. Anthropic's revised IPO filing shows roughly $895bn of compute and infrastructure commitments, which could top $1trn with other obligations. Revenue for the nine months to September reached $33.2bn, but the company warns that such rapid growth is unlikely to continue, and only about $213bn of the commitments can be avoided. Separately, the Financial Times and other outlets reported that Nvidia has told cloud partners to reduce exposure to Chinese clients, a move Nvidia has not confirmed. Palantir also reported a strong quarter, with US commercial revenue overtaking US government revenue for the first time, though its shares fell 3.1% before volatile after-hours trading.

Elsewhere, SpaceX is reportedly eyeing a purchase of Boost Mobile from EchoStar to gain tower access for Starlink phone service, though carriers have reportedly rejected earlier approaches. Across Europe, supermarket fridges and freezers were hit by a suspected cyber-attack spreading to at least seven countries, and Meta delayed new business terms after pushback over web scraping. Samsung retained the top smartphone spot in the third quarter as the overall market shrank 20%.

top_stories.title: Apple posts record iPhone quarter without a standard iPhone
top_stories.summary: Apple's quarterly iPhone revenue rose 17% to $57.58bn, driven by the iPhone 18 Pro range and price rises on older models. Total revenue reached $114.5bn, with services at $31.57bn. Ternus said memory costs were partly offset by inventory and lower component costs.

top_stories.title: Anthropic's compute commitments could top $1trn
top_stories.summary: The IPO filing reveals about $895bn in compute commitments, with more possibly to come. Growth is slowing sharply, and only about $213bn of the commitments can be avoided, raising questions about the cost base.

top_stories.title: Palantir's US commercial sales overtake government
top_stories.summary: Third-quarter revenue rose 96% to $2.31bn, ahead of forecasts, and the full-year outlook was raised. Shares still fell 3.1% on valuation and competition concerns.

top_stories.title: SpaceX reportedly eyes Boost Mobile purchase
top_stories.summary: The Washington Post reports SpaceX wants to buy Boost Mobile to extend Starlink phone coverage via leased towers. Carriers reportedly rejected earlier network access requests, and lease transfers may need their consent.

top_stories.summary: Supermarkets in at least seven countries reported fridge and freezer temperature spikes after suspected hacks. The attacks follow a French incident affecting hundreds of stores, and the EU food commissioner called them deliberate.

top_stories.summary: Omdia says Samsung shipped 57.8m phones in the third quarter, ahead of Apple's 56.5m. The overall market fell 20%, its smallest third quarter since 2013, as memory costs pushed prices up.

editions.title: Chip crunch deepens as Altman meets Samsung; Binance outflows
editions.notification: Memory chip shortage deepens as Sam Altman meets Samsung, and Binance users pull $3.6bn after its heist.
editions.intro:
The memory chip shortage dominated the last 24 hours. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman met roughly 50 Samsung executives at the company's Yongin site on Saturday, with Samsung confirming the talks covered how AI could reshape industries and business. No supply deals were announced, though memory supply is widely assumed to have been on the agenda. The meeting fits a wider pattern: Samsung and SK hynix are signing long-term customer agreements years ahead, with SK hynix saying its DRAM and HBM output is effectively sold out through 2029, yet both shares remain well below their 52-week highs.

Crypto was the other major theme. Binance users withdrew about $3.6bn as the exchange restarted services after a heist. The FBI and TRM Labs attribute the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group, and Binance says it has found further breach points. Binance has pledged to reimburse users whose assets were stolen. Separately, French lawmakers voted narrowly to add a traffic-based levy on content providers to the 2027 budget. The amendment still has to clear further budget stages, and the government opposed it.

Elsewhere, Intel and AMD may be exploring cooperation, though neither has confirmed details. Spotify is reportedly preparing an AI product with a possible premium surcharge, and Apple's first results under CEO John Ternus are due on 2 November. Most other items are rumours or product news with limited near-term market impact.

top_stories.title: Altman meets Samsung as chip crunch deepens
top_stories.summary: OpenAI's Sam Altman met Samsung's senior executives in South Korea on Saturday, with talks centred on memory chips and AI infrastructure. The meeting comes as global chip shortages intensify. No terms or commitments have been disclosed.

top_stories.summary: A narrow 11-10 committee vote added a levy of about $0.06 per gigabyte on content providers to France's 2027 budget. The measure would cover content delivery networks and still faces further budget votes, with the government opposed.

top_stories.summary: Intel's Lip-Bu Tan has discussed potential cooperation with AMD's Lisa Su, though neither company has said what it involves. Tan also said several unnamed customers want to expand foundry work, but did not confirm AMD as one.

editions.title: Amazon's AI spend, Microsoft buyouts and a neocloud wobble
editions.notification: Amazon's AWS grew 39% but free cash flow turned deeply negative. Here is why AI spending is squeezing Big Tech.
editions.intro:
Amazon dominated the period. Its third-quarter results showed Amazon Web Services growing 39% to $46bn, with a backlog of $578bn, but revenue and earnings per share came in slightly below forecasts and shares fell as much as 7% in extended trading. Free cash flow over the past year slipped to minus $42.4bn, largely from AI capital spending. Chief executive Andy Jassy said AWS should grow more than 40% in 2027 and 2028 and that Amazon will spend meaningfully more on AI next year.

The cash squeeze is a wider theme. A Reuters analysis of LSEG data finds that Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle returned the smallest share of their cash to shareholders in at least 15 years, with buybacks down 83%. Their combined capital spending of $556.9bn exceeded operating cash flow, leaving a free cash flow deficit of $14bn. Meanwhile Microsoft is offering voluntary severance to about 60,000 staff while protecting AI-critical teams, and its AI infrastructure budget is about $170bn for 2026.

Doubts about the AI build-out are growing. Shares in neocloud firms such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have fallen by about a quarter in a month, and Nvidia quietly lowered published bandwidth targets for its Vera Rubin hardware. Reports also say OpenAI has cut its fundraising target by $10bn. Against that backdrop, Oracle shares rose about 14% during its AI World conference, though they remain well below their late 2025 high.

top_stories.title: AWS grows 39% but Amazon's cash burn deepens
top_stories.summary: Amazon posted record operating margins and a 39% jump in AWS revenue, but results were slightly below forecasts and shares fell sharply after hours. Free cash flow of minus $42.4bn shows how heavily AI spending is weighing on the business, and Jassy signalled more investment in 2027.

top_stories.title: Big Tech buybacks fall 83% as AI spending outruns cash
top_stories.summary: Five hyperscalers returned the smallest share of cash to shareholders in at least 15 years. Their capex exceeded operating cash flow, with the gap funded by reserves, borrowing and share sales, despite more than $3tn in AI commitments.

top_stories.title: Microsoft offers voluntary severance to a quarter of staff
top_stories.summary: Microsoft is offering buyouts to about 60,000 employees, excluding data centres, sales, cybersecurity and quantum teams. It is the second such programme this year and comes as it keeps AI infrastructure spending near $170bn.

top_stories.title: Neocloud shares slump as bubble fears grow
top_stories.summary: CoreWeave, Nebius, IREN and Applied Digital have lost about a quarter of their value in a month, weighed by heavy debt and rising borrowing costs. A Microsoft deal cancellation and lower spending forecasts have added to the unease.

top_stories.title: Nvidia quietly trims Vera Rubin bandwidth specs
top_stories.summary: Nvidia reduced published memory and interconnect bandwidth for Vera Rubin hardware without a press release. Analysts read it as a fallback after memory suppliers struggled to hit target speeds, which could help AMD's rival parts look better on paper.

top_stories.title: OpenAI reportedly cuts fundraising target by $10bn
top_stories.summary: According to the Financial Times, OpenAI is now seeking about $20bn at a valuation near $1.25tn, a reduction that is framed as tempering ambitions amid sector anxiety. Details are limited in the available summary.

editions.title: DoorDash buys Instacart; tech sell-off deepens over AI spending
editions.notification: DoorDash agrees to buy Instacart for about $17bn as AI spending worries rattle tech stocks.
editions.intro:
The biggest development is DoorDash's agreed deal to buy rival Instacart at $65 a share, a 26% premium, valuing the business at roughly $17 billion. The cash-heavy offer still needs regulatory and shareholder approval, and it would leave iPhone users with one fewer app-based grocery and delivery option. The deal lands amid a sharp slide in US tech shares, with the Nasdaq posting its worst month since March 2025.

That selloff is driven by fears about the roughly $800 billion that Meta, Alphabet, Oracle, Amazon and Microsoft are committing to spending in 2026. Intel fell 28% after warning of weaker PC demand, while Reddit dropped 29% after weak user numbers and complaints that Google's AI search is cutting its referral traffic. Reddit's CEO said Google's AI Mode does not drive meaningful traffic, and Alphabet's core ad growth slowed to its weakest pace in five quarters even as it kept capex guidance of up to $205 billion.

The AI nervousness also shows up in private markets. The Financial Times reports that OpenAI has cut its fundraising target by $10 billion, citing the AI selloff and Anthropic's forthcoming listing; Anthropic's IPO filing, meanwhile, shows $16.3 billion of first-half revenue alongside heavy losses. Apple, by contrast, retook the title of the world's most valuable listed company, supported by iPhone demand and its China AI rollout.

top_stories.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for about $17bn
top_stories.summary: DoorDash has agreed to acquire Instacart at $65 a share, a 26% premium, with at least 75% cash consideration. The deal still needs approval and would remove one grocery delivery option for iPhone users.

top_stories.title: US tech shares slump as AI spending nears $1tn
top_stories.summary: Intel fell 28% after warning of weaker PC demand, Reddit dropped 29% and Alphabet slid further. The Nasdaq had its worst month since March 2025 as investors question heavy AI capital spending.

top_stories.summary: The FT reports OpenAI has cut its target amid an AI stock selloff and Anthropic's upcoming listing. The move could shape private AI valuations and investor appetite ahead of Anthropic's IPO.

top_stories.summary: Reddit reported search referrals fell by over a million a week in October and blamed AI Overviews and AI Mode. Reddit is also requiring logins and pushing new AI-driven feeds.

editions.title: Alphabet sheds $500bn as AI spending doubts hit Big Tech and Intel crashes
editions.notification: Alphabet loses $500bn in a day as AI spending doubts spread; Intel slumps on weak PC outlook.
editions.intro:
Investor patience with AI spending cracked this week. Alphabet lost just over $500bn in value after its quarterly update showed AI summaries in search weighing on advertising, with free cash flow negative by over $9bn. Amazon's free cash flow also swung deeply negative and its shares fell in after-hours trading, while Microsoft's shares barely moved despite 19% revenue growth. A global tech sell-off was reported to be deepening as the Nikkei and Wall Street opened lower.

Intel was the sharpest casualty. Its shares fell by roughly a quarter after third-quarter client chip revenue dropped and the company guided fourth-quarter revenue and earnings below expectations, blaming a memory shortage that is squeezing PC demand. Intel expects the PC market to shrink 12% this year. Reddit, meanwhile, said search referrals had fallen sharply and it will move to a logged-in-only experience, a direct example of how AI search is reshaping traffic.

Crypto was hit by a major security failure. Binance said an attacker drained hot wallets, with the affected amount put at about $6.3bn, and it pledged to cover losses from its SAFU fund and company money. Separately, reports that Nvidia's chief executive had ties to a Singapore businesswoman suspected by US intelligence of helping Beijing are unverified and have been strongly denied by Nvidia. Dealmaking continued, with DoorDash agreeing to buy Instacart for about $17bn and the FCC approving Amazon's Globalstar acquisition.

top_stories.title: Alphabet loses $500bn as AI search fears hit shares
top_stories.summary: Alphabet fell almost 13% to a six-month low after AI summaries in search were blamed for weaker ad revenue, even though Google Cloud grew 103%. Amazon also fell after-hours on negative free cash flow, while Microsoft held up better. The reaction shows investors increasingly questioning the payoff from heavy AI spending.

top_stories.title: Intel shares plunge after weak PC chip outlook
top_stories.summary: Intel shares fell almost a quarter after client revenue fell and fourth-quarter guidance missed estimates by a wide margin. Chief executive Lip-Bu Tan blamed memory shortages and supply constraints, and forecast the PC market shrinking 12% this year. The stock had more than doubled earlier this year, so the drop is steep.

top_stories.title: Binance hit by about $6.3bn crypto theft
top_stories.summary: Attackers drained Binance hot wallets, with the affected funds put at around $6.3bn, and Tether and Circle froze stablecoins to help. Binance says the likely entry point was a compromised engineer's laptop and has pledged to cover all customer losses. The SAFU reserve covers only a fraction of the amount, so company funds will carry much of the cost.

top_stories.title: Reddit moves to logged-in-only experience
top_stories.summary: Reddit will test a logged-in-only experience in select non-US markets from Q4, citing a drop of over a million search referrals a week. The CEO warned daily active users could fall by a low double-digit percentage in Q4 if the trend continues. Reddit still reported Q3 revenue up 53% to $895m.

top_stories.title: DoorDash to buy Instacart for $17bn
top_stories.summary: DoorDash has agreed to acquire rival Instacart at $65 per share, a 26% premium, with at least 75% in cash. The deal still needs regulatory and shareholder approval. It would consolidate two major US grocery and delivery players.

top_stories.title: Nvidia reportedly in talks to back Nscale debt
top_stories.summary: According to The Information, Nvidia is in talks to provide billions of dollars in credit guarantees for Nscale's West Virginia data centre, which Anthropic plans to use under a deal worth about $45bn. Nothing is signed and terms could change. It would make Nvidia chip supplier, equity investor and debt backer in one chain.

Finance.title: Democrats take Congress as markets sell off on AI and oil fears
Finance.notification: Democrats take the Senate and House, and markets fall on gridlock and AI worries
Finance.summary:
Democrats have won control of the US Senate and are projected to take the House in the 3 November midterms, a setback for Donald Trump. Investors have reacted with a sell-off in US stock futures, led by Nasdaq, as they weigh the risk of partisan gridlock, higher Treasury yields and a backlash against data centres that could slow the AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 has entered its third correction this year, and chip stocks have fallen across Asia and Europe.

Beyond Washington, oil remains the other big driver. Brent has been trading around $103 to $108 a barrel as US-Iran talks and Strait of Hormuz reopening hopes come and go, with Trump keeping strike options open. In Asia, the Nikkei and Kospi fell sharply on AI worries, while India's Sensex rose on Reliance's strong quarter. In the UK, the draft food standards deal with the EU is the main story, while Hamza Lemssouguer's London trading firm is in trouble.

Elsewhere, Binance is recovering from a $6.3bn hack that the FBI has linked to North Korea, and Anthropic's IPO filing has revealed large compute commitments and an operating loss. Lagarde's successor race at the ECB has formally begun.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Democrats won the Senate and are set to take the House, so Congress is likely to face gridlock. Futures fell, led by Nasdaq, on fears for AI and Treasury yields.

highlights.label: Markets
highlights.text: The Nasdaq-100 has entered its third correction this year as AI worries mount, with Nvidia and Microsoft among the decliners.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: The UK and EU have agreed a draft 200-page deal to remove many post-Brexit food and farm checks, with a UK-EU summit due later this month.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: Asian chip stocks fell as Democratic gains raised fears of AI scrutiny; Kospi dropped as much as 3.7% and Nikkei 225 fell 3.6%.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: Portugal has signed a deal to sell up to 49.9% of TAP to Lufthansa for €1.2bn, pending Brussels approval, with completion targeted for early 2028.

highlights.label: Oil
highlights.text: Brent has been trading around $103 to $108 as Hormuz reopening hopes ease prices, while Trump keeps strike options on the table.

points.text: Nominations for Lagarde's ECB successor are due by 6 November, with Hernández de Cos the front-runner on prediction markets.
China raised its FX reserve requirement by 2 points to slow the yuan's rally, though analysts see it as largely symbolic.
Reliance's quarterly profit jumped 40.6%, lifting the Sensex nearly 900 points at the open as Brent eased.
North Korea denied involvement in the $6.3bn Binance hack, which the FBI has linked to a North Korean group.
Anthropic posted a $567m operating loss on $17bn quarterly revenue, with about $895bn in compute commitments before its planned Nasdaq listing.
Large AI bond sales by US tech giants could push up borrowing costs in Europe, with France's 10-year yield near 5%.

World.title: Democrats take Congress as Iran tensions rise
World.notification: Democrats win control of Congress in the midterms as Iran strikes raise fears for oil and markets.
World.summary:
Democrats have taken control of the US Senate and are projected to win the House in the 3 November midterm elections, a result that gives them power to block Trump's agenda and open investigations. Voters cited living costs, tariffs and the war with Iran, which has pushed up fuel prices. Trump said he accepted the results and would work with Democrats, though he also warned he could veto legislation he considered insane.

The result comes as US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, described by officials as defensive, add to tension over the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of the world's oil. Diplomacy through Qatar and Pakistan continues, but Iran has warned any renewed war could be wider and longer, and oil traders are pricing in the risk.

Elsewhere, a Russian strike on an aid centre in Zaporizhzhia killed at least 26 people, and fake alerts hit air raid apps in Ukraine and Russia. In Spain, a deadly train crash has led the transport minister to resign.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Democrats won the Senate and are projected to take the House, flipping seats in Maine, Texas, Iowa and North Carolina. Trump says he will work with them.

highlights.label: Iran
highlights.text: US forces struck Qeshm Island in what officials call a defensive move. Iran warns any renewed war could be wider and last longer.

highlights.label: Florida crash
highlights.text: A Learjet 60 crashed in a residential area of Palm Beach County, killing all nine on board. About 600 residents were evacuated.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: Reports say a deal on freedom of movement with the EU could come before a summit, but any return would need a referendum and likely wait until after 2029.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: A Russian strike on an aid centre killed at least 26 people, and both Ukraine and Russia reported hacked emergency alert apps.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: Garment workers in Bangladesh are protesting for a minimum wage of 30,000 taka, with police using tear gas and dozens arrested.

points.text: Iran warned any renewed war with the US could last longer than the last, as Trump threatened further action.
The WSJ reports Iran is using guerrilla tactics, including limpet mines, to disrupt oil flows through Hormuz.
Spain's transport minister will resign after a train crash that killed 69 people, the second deadly rail crash in under a year.
Fake nuclear and chemical alerts hit Ukraine's air raid app on Sunday; Moscow said its own warning app was hit by a cyberattack.
The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate to 4.85%, but its statement was seen as dovish, pointing to fewer hikes.
Western officials say British troops would be allowed to return fire if attacked during a future peacekeeping mission in Ukraine.

Tech.title: Cyber-attacks hit European fridges as AI chip and tech earnings dominate
Tech.notification: Supermarket freezers hit by cyber-attacks across seven European countries as temperatures climb to 50C.
Tech.summary:
A suspected cyber-attack has disrupted refrigeration and freezer systems at supermarkets in at least seven European countries, with temperatures reportedly rising as high as 50C overnight. Ahold Delhaize, Ikea, Carrefour Belgium, Colruyt and SuperValu are among those affected, and some shops have pulled chilled and frozen goods from sale. It follows a French attack last month that reportedly hit up to 700 supermarkets. The EU food commissioner has called the attacks a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.

Elsewhere, the chip and AI theme dominated earnings. AMD reported a record quarter, with data centre revenue of $8.5 billion and guidance of $17 billion for next quarter, while Apple's iPhone revenue rose 17% to $57.58 billion despite no standard iPhone launch. Demand for AI infrastructure is pulling in memory and chip supply, which is raising prices for phones and PCs and squeezing consumer segments such as gaming and PC shipments.

Concerns over AI spending have also been visible in markets. The Nasdaq briefly entered correction territory before recovering, and reports of Oracle dropping a $7 billion Tencent AI deal and Nvidia asking cloud clients to cut China exposure show how US policy is shaping AI business. Anthropic's IPO filing, which shows around $895 billion in compute commitments, underlines the scale of the spending involved.

highlights.text: iPhone revenue reached $57.58bn, up 17%, driven by the pricier iPhone 18 Pro. The foldable iPhone Duo sold out soon after launch.

highlights.text: Record quarter with $13.4bn revenue and data centre at about 63% of sales. Next-quarter guidance is $17bn, but gaming fell 40%.

Fashion.title: Estée Lauder lifts outlook as fragrance drives recovery
Fashion.notification: Estée Lauder raises its forecast as fragrance surges 20% and margins widen. Here is what it means for the sector.
Fashion.summary:
Estée Lauder Companies has given the luxury beauty sector one of its clearest signs of recovery this season. Net sales rose 6% in the first quarter, fragrance jumped 20% on the strength of Le Labo, Tom Ford, Jo Malone London and Kilian Paris, and the company lifted its fiscal 2027 growth forecast to 4 to 5.5%. Adjusted operating margin improved sharply to 12.1% from 7.3%, and Asia-Pacific grew 10%, with mainland China up 9%.

The results sit within a wider reshaping of the premium sector. Chief executive Stéphane de La Faverie said the company is spending more on consumer-facing marketing as part of its turnaround, a sign that growth is being bought as well as earned. Haircare was flat because of a supply chain problem at Aveda, a reminder that operational fragility still hits the numbers.

Elsewhere, the mood is more mixed. Hugo Boss cut its outlook on weaker demand and higher costs, and the Financial Times reports a junk-debt sell-off that is weighing on credit investors. Luxury houses are still active in marketing and sustainability, with Kering opening a water resilience lab in Italy and Burberry launching its festive campaign for its 170th anniversary.

highlights.text: Anthony Vaccarello was named International Designer of the Year at the CFDA Awards, marking a decade at Saint Laurent. Tory Burch and Gap also won honours.

highlights.label: Kering
